slides: In the last question, the shaded triangle was exactly as big as the two white triangles together. Let's take that idea and stretch it.

slides.say: A rectangle, and a diagonal in it. The diagonal cuts the rectangle into two triangles, and they are exactly the same size. So the shaded half equals the white half, and each one is half of the rectangle.

Now a shaded triangle inside a rectangle, like in the last question. Its base is the bottom side, and its tip, E, is on the top side. Here too, the shaded part is half of the rectangle, and the white parts together are the other half.
Why? From E, drop a height down to the bottom side. It cuts the rectangle into two smaller rectangles, and each small rectangle has a diagonal.

In the left rectangle, the shaded piece and the white piece are the two halves, so they're equal. In the right rectangle too. So each shaded piece equals its white twin. The same colour means the same area.
And it doesn't matter where E is along the top side. Move it, and the shaded triangle is still half of the rectangle.

Now three shaded triangles in a rectangle. Their tips are on the top side, and their bases sit one after the other on the bottom side. The triangles do not overlap, and their bases cover the whole bottom side without gaps.
at: Their tips are on the top side

slides.say: Why is the shaded part still half? All three triangles have the same height, the height of the rectangle. So each area is its base times h, over two. And the three bases together make the whole bottom side. So the sum is the whole base times h, over two, which is half of the rectangle.
at: All three triangles have the same height

slides.say: By the way, this isn't only true in a rectangle. It's true in the whole parallelogram family: a parallelogram, a rectangle, a rhombus and a square. A diagonal in a parallelogram also cuts it into two triangles with the same area.
And this one? A shaded triangle on the bottom side of a parallelogram, with its tip on the top side. It's harder to see, but from the tip, draw a line parallel to the slanted sides.
Now we have two parallelograms, a left one and a right one. In each of them, the shaded piece and the white piece are the two halves. So the shaded triangle is half of the whole parallelogram.

Its height is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel sides, not the slanted line we drew. Same base and same height, the same area. And several triangles work too, as long as they don't overlap and their bases cover the bottom side without gaps.
at: Its height is the perpendicular distance

slides.say: A slightly more advanced one. The bottom side is cut into four equal pieces. The shaded triangle stands on one piece, and its tip is on the top side. What part of the rectangle is it?

A triangle on the whole bottom side, with its tip on the top side, would be half of the rectangle. Ours has the same height, but it stands on only a quarter of the bottom side. So it's a quarter of that half.
at: A triangle on the whole bottom side
So it's a quarter of that half

slides.say: A quarter of a half is an eighth. So the shaded triangle is an eighth of the rectangle.

slides: This symmetry principle is very important. Some exam questions become easy with it, and we'll see one in the next question. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
